answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — no source in her writings
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · circulating online as Woolf’s by January 2016
answer.sourceLine: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ lists this line with “Source: None,” and Woolf scholar Stuart N. Clarke called it made up in 2018. Nobody has identified who first wrote it. By January 2016 it was already being passed around online with Woolf’s name on it.

source.excerpt: A feminist is any woman who tells the truth about her life.
trail: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain’s misquotations page ↗ lists the line with “Source: None.” It notes thousands of occurrences online, including one academic journal, and observes that “Woolf is known as a feminist, so it is convenient to credit her.”

In April 2018 a scholar on the Vwoolf mailing list (archived April 2018 thread) ↗ said they could not find the line anywhere in Woolf’s writing. Stuart N. Clarke replied “It’s madey-uppy,” and later annotated it as “MADE UP, but cf. the speech of 21 Jan. 1931 in ‘The Pargiters’.”

A BUST listicle dated 25 January 2016 (Wayback capture) ↗, “30 Virginia Woolf Photos And Quotes In Celebration Of Her Birthday” by Olivia Harrison, opens with the line. On the Vwoolf list, Clarke identified this piece as the reference an academic book review gave for the quotation.

The nearest genuine Woolf passage on the theme comes from “Professions for Women,” collected in The Death of the Moth, and Other Essays ↗: “telling the truth about my own experiences as a body, I do not think I solved.”
source.excerptNote: No text by Woolf contains this sentence. The Woolf Society suggests that the nearest genuine line is in “The Leaning Tower”: “If you do not tell the truth about yourself you cannot tell it about other people.”

source.rightsNote: The wording can’t be traced to Woolf or to any other identifiable author or work, so we make no copyright claim about it. Woolf’s real lines quoted on this page come from essays first published in 1940 (“The Leaning Tower”) and 1942 (The Death of the Moth). Neither date falls before 1931.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Virginia Woolf wrote Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and A Room of One’s Own, and is one of the central figures of literary modernism. Readers know her as a feminist, and the Woolf Society notes that this is why unsourced lines about women are so “convenient” to credit to her. Her real writing on truth-telling, such as “Professions for Women” and “The Leaning Tower,” is more qualified than the slogan.

misattribution.heading: How the line got pinned on Woolf
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely shared “Woolf” quotations online. It is short and feminist and it suits her reputation, but nobody has found it in her novels, essays, letters or diaries.

items.why: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ gives “Source: None” for this line and suggests her fame as a feminist is what makes the credit “convenient.”
A birthday round-up of Woolf quotations opens with the line ↗ and gives no source. In 2018 Clarke annotated this list’s version as “MADE UP.”

items.who: A book review in the International Feminist Journal of Politics
items.why: According to the Vwoolf list discussion ↗, this review opens with the quotation and cites the BUST listicle (“Harrison 2017”) as its source, not any work by Woolf.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence does not appear anywhere in Woolf’s writing. According to the Woolf Society ↗, the closest genuine line is from “The Leaning Tower” (1940): “If you do not tell the truth about yourself you cannot tell it about other people.”

context.heading: What Woolf actually wrote about truth-telling
lead: Woolf did write about how hard it is for a woman to tell the truth about her own life. She did not put it as a slogan. In “Professions for Women,” first given as a talk in 1931 to the London branch of the National Society for Women’s Service ↗, she says she managed to kill “the Angel in the House,” but that telling the truth about her own experiences as a body remained unsolved: “I doubt that any woman has solved it yet.”

Woolf was also wary of the word “feminist” itself. In Three Guineas ↗ (1938) she proposes to destroy “a vicious and corrupt word”: “The word ‘feminist’ is the word indicated.” A Vwoolf list member made the same point in 2018, arguing that a writer who said this was unlikely to define a feminist the way the internet quote does.
context.detailsSummary: Why scholars point to a 1931 speech
detailsBody: When Stuart N. Clarke annotated the BUST list in 2018, he marked this line “MADE UP,” but added “cf. the speech of 21 Jan. 1931 in ‘The Pargiters’.” That speech is the talk that became “Professions for Women.” The theme is related, but the sentence is not Woolf’s.

Quote Investigator has no article on this line, and the line is not among the sourced quotations on Wikiquote’s Woolf page ↗. That page sends readers to the Woolf Society’s misquotations list for further examples.

Clarke replied 'It's madey-uppy'; Jeremy Hawthorn found an IFJP book review opening with it; Clarke identified its reference as Harrison, Olivia. 2017. '30 Virginia Woolf Photos And Quotes...' BUST listicle '30 Virginia Woolf Photos And Quotes In Celebration Of Her Birthday' by Olivia Harrison, datePublished January 25, 2016, opens with 'A feminist is any woman who tells the truth about her life.'

The Death of the Moth, and Other Essays contains 'Professions for Women' ('A paper read to The Women's Service League') with the passage 'telling the truth about my own experiences as a body, I do not think I solved. I doubt that any woman has solved it yet.'
Woolf first gave 'Professions for Women' as a talk in 1931 to the London branch of the National Society for Women's Service
Three Guineas contains: 'What more fitting than to destroy an old word, a vicious and corrupt word... The word 'feminist' is the word indicated.'

Wikiquote's Virginia Woolf page does not list this line among its sourced quotes, dates Three Guineas (1938) and The Death of the Moth and Other Essays (1942), and links to the VWSGB Misquotations and Misattributions page
